youtube_title: Why Your Cruise Between U.S. Ports Stops in Another Country 🦝⚖️
caption: Under the Passenger Vessel Services Act regulations, a non-U.S.-qualified ship can sail a round trip from one U.S. port with a nearby foreign stop — but ending at a different U.S. port needs a distant foreign port.
script: Why would a cruise between American ports bother stopping in another country? Sometimes, the law explains it. This is the Passenger Vessel Services Act, a U.S. law that limits carrying passengers between U.S. ports on ships that aren't qualified for that domestic trade, like foreign-flagged cruise ships. Customs regulations spell out how it works. If a cruise only visits U.S. ports, and passengers get off at a U.S. port, that's a violation. Now add a nearby foreign port, like one in Canada, Mexico, the Bahamas or the Caribbean. If passengers end the trip back at the same U.S. port where they boarded, the regulations don't treat that as a violation. That's one reason round-trip cruises often include a quick foreign stop. But if passengers end the trip at a different U.S. port, a nearby foreign stop isn't enough. The ship would need to visit a distant foreign port, one outside that nearby list. There are special cases too, like Puerto Rico. Here's the limit. A foreign stop doesn't make every itinerary legal, and this is the passenger rule, not the Jones Act rules for cargo. Cruise lines can ask Customs for an advisory ruling, and nothing here means any particular route is approved. [loop] So the next time your cruise makes a surprise stop abroad, remember
